help.intro: sein and haben are the two verbs Germans do not put into the Perfekt when they talk about the past: they say ich war (not ich bin gewesen) and ich hatte (not ich habe gehabt). You learnt the forms earlier in the course; here they do a job — they carry the background of a story while the Perfekt carries the events. Das Wetter war schön, ich hatte viel Zeit, also bin ich an den See gefahren. States, feelings, weather, possession, age: war and hatte. Actions: Perfekt. Get that split right and your past-tense stories sound German instead of translated.
help.tips[0].title: war / hatte for background, Perfekt for events
help.tips[0].text: Es war kalt (state) — ich habe einen Mantel gekauft (event). Ich hatte Hunger (state) — ich habe gegessen (event). The story is told with both, in that division of labour.
help.tips[0].examples[0].en: Yesterday I was ill and had a temperature. I went to the doctor.
help.tips[0].examples[1].en: The concert was great, we had good seats.
help.tips[0].check.q: Es war kalt, also habe ich einen Mantel gekauft. Which part is the background state?
help.tips[0].check.why: The weather is a state, so it takes war; buying the coat is the event, told in the Perfekt.
help.tips[0].visual.caption: The background stretches under the story; the events are points on it.
help.tips[1].title: The full paradigms
help.tips[1].text: war, warst, war, waren, wart, waren · hatte, hattest, hatte, hatten, hattet, hatten. First and third person identical; the rest take -st, -en, -t, -en.
help.tips[1].examples[0].en: Where were you? – We were in the park. Did you have fun? – Yes, lots.
help.tips[1].examples[1].en: Were you at the cinema yesterday? – No, I didn't have time.
help.tips[2].title: Prefer war and hatte to gewesen and gehabt
help.tips[2].text: ich bin gewesen and ich habe gehabt exist and you will read and hear them (Bist du schon einmal in Wien gewesen?), but in everyday speech war and hatte are shorter and far more common. Wie war dein Tag? Es war gut. Ich hatte keine Zeit.
help.tips[2].examples[0].en: Have you been to Italy? – Yes, I was in Rome last year.
help.tips[2].examples[1].en: How was your day? – It was good, but I had a lot of work.
help.tips[2].trap: resist translating every 'I have been' with the Perfekt. war is the natural form; gewesen is the exception.
help.tips[2].check.q: Wie ____ dein Wochenende? – Sehr schön, danke!
help.tips[2].check.why: Asking how something was uses war, the short everyday past of sein.
help.tips[3].text: Childhood is told with war / hatte: Als Kind war ich klein und hatte einen Hund. It is the first place learners meet Präteritum as storytelling — later in the course it extends to every verb.
help.tips[3].examples[0].en: As a child I had many friends and was always outside.
help.tips[3].examples[1].en: As a child I had a dog, and I was often in the park with him.
help.tips[3].check.why: Owning something is haben, and childhood is told in the past: ich hatte.
help.remember[0]: war and hatte paint the scene; the Perfekt moves the action.
help.remember[1]: 'Es war schön' — prefer war to 'Es ist schön gewesen' when you talk.
help.context.en: Last weekend I was in Dresden. The weather was bad and I had no umbrella, so I bought one. In the evening we were at a concert – the music was fantastic, and we had seats right at the front. On Sunday I unfortunately had a headache and went home early.
help.mistakes[0].why: States use war in everyday German.
help.mistakes[1].why: haben in the past is hatte.
help.hook: Tell a story the way Germans do: war and hatte set the scene — Es war kalt, ich hatte Hunger — and the Perfekt moves it on.
help.recall.known: From "war & hatte": all the forms of war and hatte.
help.recall.today: When to use them: war and hatte paint the background, the Perfekt tells the events.
sentences[0].why: sein's past: ich war — bare, with no ending.
sentences[2].why: er/sie/es shares ich's bare form: war.
sentences[4].why: haben's past: ich hatte — double t, no extra ending.
sentences[5].why: meine Oma = sie, and er/sie/es is hatte — same as ich.
sentences[6].english: We had a lot of fun.
sentences[7].english: Where were you (all) in the summer?
sentences[8].why: du adds -st: hattest — and the question starts with the verb.
sentences[9].english: He was not in the office yesterday.
sentences[9].why: er takes the bare past: war.
sentences[10].english: My parents had a small house.
sentences[12].english: As a child I had many friends.
sentences[12].why: ich hatte — Als Kind fills position 1, the verb stays second.
sentences[14].english: Have you been to Vienna, Mr Braun?
sentences[15].english: Why were you in such a bad mood yesterday?
sentences[16].english: Have you (all) ever been to Hamburg?
sentences[16].why: ihr's form of war ends in -t: Wart ihr.
sentences[17].english: Last winter we had no luck with the weather.
sentences[17].why: wir takes hatten — plural past of haben.
